title: Live: Minister accuses Coalition of being 'juvenile' for AI office criticism
description: Tim Ayres has accused the Coalition of being "juvenile" for criticising the establishment of an Office of AI in the prime minister's department. Follow live.
content_snippet: Industry and Science Minister Tim Ayres is out spruiking the federal government's new artificial intelligence standards. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese yesterday announced plans for mandatory rules…
author: Joshua Boscaini
full_text: Federal politics: PM defends breaking last year's promise to attend Garma Festival — as it happened Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has defended his decision to break a promise by not attending the Garma Festival this year. Take a look back at the day's coverage below. LoadingThu 16 Jul 2026 at 1:08pm Greens welcome govt's move to toughen modern slavery penalties The Greens have welcomed the federal government's move to toughen modern slavery laws. Major companies that fail to prevent modern slavery in their supply chains will be prosecuted under a government proposal to toughen Australia's modern slavery laws. The criminal offence would apply to companies with an annual consolidated revenue of more than $100 million. Greens senator David Shoebridge says it would be a "genuine step forward" and has pledged to work with Labor on the legislation. "Australia imports nearly $100 billion of goods with a high risk of slavery in their supply chain every year. This isn't an academic issue, it can mean life and death for millions of exploited workers," Shoebridge says. "This is urgent reform and the Greens intend to work with the government to ensure this legislation delivers on the promise." Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 11:50am Analysis: Albanese welcomes AI companies to Australia on our terms. We just don't know what those are yet Prime Minister Anthony Albanese chose an intriguing backdrop for his much-hyped speech on how Australia will respond to the AI boom. It was hard to ignore. Both literally, because a giant plastic #USYD sign took up a great portion of the stage, but also because the prime minister began with a reflection on his formative years at the institution. The choice of venue was ostensibly because the University of Sydney's researchers and students are embracing AI. They're using it in research, they're making commercial products with it, and they're adapting their teaching to it. What went unmentioned, perhaps understandably, is the way that AI is turning the university sector upside down. AI-assisted cheating is rampant, educators are being forced to redesign curricula on the fly, and there are fears their use may stop students from developing their own skills if misused. Read the full analysis from national AI reporter Cam Wilson in the link below. Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 11:41am Australia's last manganese smelter in Tasmania to close In some breaking news this morning, the administrators of Australia's last manganese smelter say they have ordered the immediate closure of the business. The Liberty Bell Bay smelter in northern Tasmania was placed into administration in March this year, but in May administrators announced they had entered into an agreement with a consortium to acquire the business. In a joint statement with the Tasmanian premier, Industry Minister Tim Ayres says the closure is a "very sad day" for northern Tasmania. "This is deeply difficult news for the workers of Liberty Bell Bay and the communities of Bell Bay, George Town and northern Tasmania who have fought tirelessly for a better outcome," the statement says. "Both the Commonwealth and Tasmanian governments are now focused on ensuring workers and their families are supported during this time, with immediate on-ground support now available." Read the full story from our colleagues in Tasmania for the full details. Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 11:36am Angus Taylor backs in Jacinta Nampijinpa Price following social media repost Angus Taylor has repeated that a Liberal frontbencher's repost of a right-wing podcaster's tweet is not an endorsement of a position. The Australian reported this week that Jacinta Nampijinpa Price shared a 2 Worlds Collide post that claims Labor is importing migrants from India, Africa and the Middle East for electoral gain. Earlier today, the opposition leader said he had spoken to Nampijinpa Price but not about that issue. Speaking in Melbourne, Taylor says the NT Liberal senator believes that getting immigration policy settings right in Australia is important. "Jacinta, like me and Jane, believe that immigration policy is hugely important to get right in this country. The numbers have been too high and the standards have been too low and the numbers must change." And that's it from the opposition leader's press conference in Melbourne. Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 11:26am Angus Taylor not supportive of gender quotas despite Liberal discussion paper Angus Taylor and Jane Hume have stepped up for a press conference in Melbourne following a meeting with the Chinese business community. He's been asked about a Liberal Party discussion paper that has called upon its aging membership base to provide ideas on how to modernise and take the party forward. The paper canvassed a number of options, including gender quotas, open preselections and new membership models. Taylor says he's never supported quotas, but instead supports initiatives that will get a broader range of people into the party. "I strongly support that regeneration, rebuild of the party that we need, because this country needs a strong Liberal Party," Taylor says. "We also need to make sure there's policies for young Australians, like ensuring that there is hope that they can buy and own a home and start a business and raise a family." The deputy Liberal leader says she wants to ensure that the organisational wing of the party is "match fit and ready" to fight elections. Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 10:41am Liberals canvas ideas to address gender, youth and 'deep-rooted' multicultural problem The Liberals are calling upon their aging membership base to provide ideas on how to modernise and take the party forward after back-to-back election disasters. In a discussion paper sent to party faithful, respondents were urged to engage in a "reality check," acknowledging that by the next election, almost one in five voters will have been born after the year 2000. "Realistically, they will have no historical memory of September 11, the Howard government [or] a world without smartphones," the paper said. In the wake of the 2025 election loss, the Liberals established a commission to embark on a soul-searching mission on how to win back voters. In a paper emailed on Wednesday, the commission argued the party's base must think outside its usual playbook to bounce back from the second-lowest primary vote in its history last election. Read the full story from political reporters Ewa Staszewska and Holly Tregenza in the link below. Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 9:47am AI office urged to include artists after Anthony Albanese's copyright promise Australian artists want a seat around the table at the new office for artificial intelligence established by Anthony Albanese in a bid to "shape" how the technology affects the country. The prime minister has pledged writers and musicians will retain control over if and how their work is used to train AI, allaying industry fears the federal government was poised to dilute copyright laws in order to attract data centre investment. Albanese on Wednesday also announced plans for mandatory rules around water and power usage for data centres and signalled a more coordinated approach to other AI challenges to be run through a new office in his department. In a speech in Sydney, he promised Australia's laws "will spell … out" clear protections for creatives who permit AI to train on their books, music and art, and also implied further work to come on the copyright issue. Read the full story from chief digital political correspondent Clare Armstrong in the link below. Key Event Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 9:13am PM defends decision not to attend Garma Festival Anthony Albanese has defended his decision to break a promise and not attend this year's Garma Festival in the Northern Territory. The prime minister last year committed to attending every Garma Festival every single year while holding the office of PM. Albanese says he hasn't had a day off all year, and that he'll be at another festival in the NT later this week. "I haven't had a day off all year. All year. And this weekend, in a few days, I'll be in another remote part of the Northern Territory," Albanese says. "I will be at another festival in the Northern Territory in [the] coming days, and I've been to Garma every year that it's been held since I've been Labor leader in 2019." Key Event Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 9:08am Albanese says national AI standards will only apply to new data centres The prime minister says the legislated national artificial intelligence standards will only apply to new data centre developments. Anthony Albanese says the rules will apply to "very large" data centres, which he says could be built in "inappropriate locations". "What we're saying is we'll codify that, will provide that clarity, that certainty, and what that will do is to provide certainty; that is the number one thing that investors look for," Albanese says. Albanese says the government doesn't want to see a "free-for-all" on the construction of data centres. He says there needs to be a social licence for their construction. Key Event Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 8:58am PM says new AI national standards aim to protect property of artists, creatives Anthony Albanese has phoned into ABC Radio Sydney to talk about his speech yesterday on the federal government's national AI framework. The PM announced yesterday a set of legislated national standards with mandatory rules for data centres on water and power usage. The standards will also ensure that artists and creatives retain control over their work when it is used to build or train AI. Albanese says the new standards aim to protect the intellectual property of artists and creatives, and ensure that their content can't be used to train AI without consent. "Part of that will be a recognition that artists' creativity, whether it be writers or songwriters or other people in the creative sector, including the media, that their work is their property and that it can't be used without one, control and secondly, without payment," Albanese says. Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 8:42am Attorney-general says Australian creatives will have seat at table on AI Attorney-General Michelle Rowland says Australian artists and creatives will have a seat at the table to ensure they can "thrive" in the AI economy. Australian artists have welcomed Labor's artificial intelligence copyright pledge and say they want input at a new office coordinating a national response to the technology. The PM announced yesterday that new legislated AI standards will ensure Australian artists and creatives retain control over their work to build or train AI. Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Rowland says the government's primary focus is the importance of preserving Australian culture. "That's the basis for a copyright regime that has served Australia well, and again, this is a property right that has been around for a very long time. It has been very durable at various ages of technological development," Rowland says. "Creatives will be coming to the table to look at ways at which we can ensure they are getting properly recompensed and also that they can thrive in the new AI economy." Key Event Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 8:17am Joyce says he doesn't agree with what far-right podcaster, who met with Hanson, does One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce says he doesn't support much of what a far-right UK podcaster, who met with his party leader last week, does. Tommy Robinson, born Stephen Christopher Yaxley-Lennon, is a prominent far-right, anti-Islam, anti-migration activist in the UK. He met with Pauline Hanson last week during her visit to the UK and sat down with the One Nation leader for an interview, which is yet to be released. Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Joyce says while he thinks it's worth understanding his views, he won't seek to replicate the activist. "I don't support so much of what Tommy Robinson does, but I think it's incredibly important we understand the social dynamic and how that came about," Joyce says. "If I had the opportunity to talk to him, I would [want] to work out exactly what was going on in their head." Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 7:54am Rowland won't say whether tougher modern slavery laws are linked to new US tariffs The attorney-general hasn't said whether the introduction of tougher modern slavery penalties is linked with new US tariffs. As we've reported, major companies that fail to prevent modern slavery in their supply chains will be prosecuted under new tougher laws. In June, the US proposed hitting Australia with a new 12.5 per cent tariff for failing to crack down on goods made with forced labour. But speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Michelle Rowland says the federal government has been undertaking a long period of consultation on the tougher laws. "On the issue of tariffs, we have consistently made the case to the United States that any tariffs on Australian products are unjustified," Rowland says. "What we've announced today in terms of our modern slavery reforms, they follow extensive consultation and I think that they will be widely welcomed by Australians." Key Event Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 7:39am Angus Taylor defends Liberal frontbencher's retweet of right-wing podcaster's post Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says he doesn't think a Liberal frontbencher's retweet of a social media video from a right-wing podcaster equals an endorsement of a position. The Australian reported Jacinta Nampijinpa Price shared a 2 Worlds Collide post that claims Labor is importing migrants from India, Africa and the Middle East for electoral gain. Speaking to Channel Nine, Taylor says he's been in touch with Nampijinpa Price over recent days but hasn't spoken to her about this issue. "A retweet is not an endorsement," Taylor says. "A retweet is pointing to a post that is made by someone else with obvious questions." Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 7:30am Australia to toughen modern slavery rules Major companies that fail to prevent modern slavery in their supply chains will be prosecuted under a government proposal to toughen Australia's modern slavery laws. The criminal offence would apply to companies with an annual consolidated revenue of more than $100 million, though a defence will be available if companies can demonstrate they took reasonable steps to prevent worker exploitation. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland says the government will work closely with stakeholders to design Labor's proposed legislation . "Australians rightly expect that the products they buy are not made on the back of modern slavery, which is why the Albanese government is delivering a legislative framework with teeth," she says. "The proposed changes will introduce greater accountability, levelling the playing field for the majority of Australian businesses already doing the right thing." According to the Global Slavery Index, an estimated 50 million people are living in modern slavery, which includes forced labour and debt bondage. Key Event Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 7:29am Tim Ayres says move to legislate AI standards is 'evolution' Industry Minister Tim Ayres says the federal government's shift from artificial intelligence guidelines to legislated standards is an "evolution" in the way Labor approaches AI. The PM unveiled the government's approach to AI at a speech yesterday, with mandatory rules for data centres to form part of new legislated standards. Those standards will force new data centres to minimise their water usage, underwrite new electricity generation and pay the full cost of connecting to the grid. Asked whether he supports the Greens proposal for a moratorium on new data centres until the standards have been introduced, Ayres says it's a "pretty dopey" idea that would take Australia backwards. "We cannot afford to stand still. We cannot afford to stand still as a country. The data centre expectations are being worked through with the states," Ayres tells the ABC's AM program. "Key tech firms [are] signing memorandums of understanding with the government that are consistent with those. We are going to move to make them mandatory. It's very clear to see the direction of travel here." Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 7:14am Coalition says govt needs to admit implementation of aged care reforms is wrong Shadow Aged Care Minister Anne Ruston says the government needs to admit that it's getting it wrong with the implementation of aged care reforms. Australia's outgoing aged care inspector Natalie Siegel-Brown told the National Press Club yesterday the way the government's overhaul of the aged care system is being implemented is causing harm. The shadow minister says she thinks the infrastructure through which the legislation is being delivered needs to be examined. Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Ruston says the Coalition is prepared to work with the government to make the necessary changes. "To have a situation where 200,000 older Australians are either waiting for the care they've been assessed as needing or waiting for an assessment means that [there are] 200,000 older Australians whose health conditions are deteriorating while they're waiting to get care," Ruston says. Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 7:09am Ayres says Coalition criticism of new AI office is 'juvenile' Industry and Science Minister Tim Ayres is out spruiking the federal government's new artificial intelligence standards. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese yesterday announced plans for mandatory rules around water and power usage for data centres. He also announced the creation of an Office of AI to sit within the PM's department, which will coordinate the design of the AI standards. Speaking to Channel Nine, Ayres says the standards show "Australia doing artificial intelligence the Australian way". But asked about criticism from the Coalition that the new office is another level of bureaucracy, Ayres says the opposition is negative. "There's a big set of challenges and opportunities here for Australia in artificial intelligence. We've set up an Office of Artificial Intelligence in the Office of the Prime Minister," Ayres says. "All poor old Angus Taylor can do is complain about public servants doing this work. I mean it's just juvenile, it's partisan, it's unsurprising."
